workingTitle: A tiny dragon egg may hold the seed of a massive star
publicationStatus: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics; public arXiv preprint
coreFacts: ALMA Band 6 observations resolved the C2c1 region in the dragon cloud at about 175 to 400 astronomical units.
The brightest component, C2c1a(a), remains a single compact continuum peak down to about 175 astronomical units, with a deconvolved radius near 87 astronomical units.
Its brightness temperature is about 39 to 40 kelvins, above the roughly 10 kelvin temperature inferred at lower resolution.
Continuum-based mass estimates span roughly 1.9 to 12.8 solar masses under the measured brightness-temperature assumption, while a colder 10-kelvin assumption permits about 30 solar masses.
The compact source lies inside a larger cold reservoir containing roughly 100 to 110 solar masses on scales near 10,000 astronomical units.
caveats: The dust temperature is uncertain, so the compact peak may be a cold massive core or a warmer lower-mass component.
No robust outflow is associated with the peak, but a weak, deeply embedded, or unfavourably oriented outflow cannot be excluded.
The observations do not prove that the core is starless and do not uniquely distinguish monolithic core accretion from continued growth out of the surrounding reservoir.
No additional compact fragments were detected only within the present resolution and sensitivity limits.
